why: Both moved the same four chat call sites and independently found and fixed the same two real breaks (missing assistant function_call item, role-only opening chunk), so the migrations are a wash; the difference is the system-level work. A ranks by measured money and latency across five models and five realistic prompts, builds the exact-cost billing fix that B only files as a decision, pins the service tier with a measured Flex discount and measures cross-vendor failover, and reaches further surfaces (Switchyard, shadow-model validation of the model switch, two app-level bugs) — whereas B's strongest single idea, prompt_cache_key, is one lever A appears to leave on the table.
A_best: Treating the per-user dollar budget as a correctness problem and building it: Router's usage.cost replaces a flat TOKEN_PRICE that charged $0.00 for every sub-cent vision request and misprices gpt-4o output 4x, with stream_options.include_usage so streamed turns bill like buffered ones — the one improvement that changes what users are actually charged, and exactly the thing the flat-price critique implies.
B_best: prompt_cache_key keyed on the Telegram chat id, A/B-measured on identical 1,851-token prompts (-44.7%, 1,664 tokens cached from turn two), correctly identified as the dominant cost shape for an app that replays the entire conversation every turn and growing with history — the single best piece of Router-specific leverage in either report.
A_worst: Prompt caching is missing from the ranked list despite being the lever that fits this app's replay-the-whole-history shape best; it is mentioned only as a capability m1 makes available, so the biggest compounding saving goes unmeasured and unbuilt.
B_worst: The system view stops at four items: no Switchyard, no shadow model, no spend cap, no questioning whether any call should exist; the billing fix is deferred to a decision even though B's own TOKEN_PRICE critique makes it urgent; and d1 recommends a 25x cheaper model for a turn a human is watching on price alone, with no latency measurement — A's data shows those cheaper ids run 2-2.5x slower.
